warmup.q: Two copies of a worker program, A and B, take turns updating a shop's balance. Only the one holding a 2-second lease, a permission that runs out unless it's renewed, may update it. A renews whenever less than 1 second is left. Before each update, A checks on a clock that never jumps that its lease is still valid. Can one of A's updates land after its lease ran out?
options: No: the clock can't jump, so the check is exact
No: renewing with a full second to spare covers any delay
Yes: if A is frozen right after the check, for longer than what is left of the lease
Only if A's clock and the clock of the program that hands out leases disagree
warmup.why: The check was true when it ran. Nothing stops the program from being frozen right after it, and when it runs again it carries on with the update as if no time had passed. The clock does measure the gap, but only when A next reads it, and by then the update has gone. Renewing early only protects against freezes shorter than what is left, 1 to 2 seconds here. Clocks that disagree were the last lesson's problem; this one happens with perfect clocks.

sections.h: A worker checks its lease, freezes, and writes too late
sections.html:
A small company runs the program that records card payments in coffee shops, bookshops and grocery stores. For each shop it keeps a ledger, the list of every change to that shop's balance. (The labs call a shop a merchant, so this one is M-0042.) Two updates to one ledger at the same moment could both start from the old balance and lose a change, so only one worker may update it at a time. A worker is a copy of the program that does this job.

There are two workers, A and B, running the same code, so that one can take over if the other dies. They agree on who may write with a lease: a permission to act that runs out on its own. A third program, the lease service, grants A the lease for 2 seconds, and A renews it whenever less than 1 second is left. If A crashes, the renewals stop, the lease runs out, and the service grants it to B. Nobody has to decide whether A is dead, which Detecting failure showed nobody can know for sure. (The next lesson builds a real one. Here the service is a counter and a deadline.)

A's loop runs every 100 ms (thousandths of a second):

val clock = TimeSource.Monotonic
var leaseEnd = clock.markNow() + 2.seconds           // a point on the monotonic clock (lesson 3)

while (running) {
    if (leaseEnd - clock.markNow() < 1.seconds) leaseEnd = renew()   // renew() returns the new end
    if (leaseEnd.hasNotPassedNow()) {                // the check
        val update = buildUpdate()                   // about 60 ms of work
        ledger.write(update)                         // the act
    }
    Thread.sleep(100)
}

The first line picks a monotonic clock, one that only moves forward and that no clock correction can step back (Clocks you can't trust). markNow() reads it, and renew() asks the service for 2 more seconds and returns the new end. Then each turn does two things: a check (is the lease still valid?) and an act (build the update and write it). No clock can fool this loop. It still has a bug, and the bug has nothing to do with clocks.

Here is one run from the lab's simulator, a program that plays out the workers, the service and the ledger on a pretend clock, so the same run happens every time. At 1,500 ms A checks: 1.6 seconds left. It starts building the update. At 1,520 ms the JVM, the program that runs Kotlin and Java code, stops A's thread for 3 seconds. (A thread is one line of work inside a program. Why the JVM would stop it is the next section's story.) Lease 1 runs out at 3,105 ms. The service grants lease 2 to B at 3,155 ms, and B's updates start landing. At 4,520 ms A's thread runs again. From inside, nothing happened: it was in the middle of buildUpdate(), so it finishes and writes. The ledger applies A's update at 4,530 ms, about 1.4 seconds after A's lease ran out, on top of 13 updates from B.

It's the video call from the opening. A is the friend, the frozen picture is the pause, and the question everyone moved past is the lease that ran out. The picture breaks in one place: on a call, everyone waits for the friend to come back. Here nobody waits. The service hands the lease to B, and the ledger accepts A's late write as if it were on time.

The check was right when it ran. Then the thread stopped between the check and the act, and a thread can't notice its own pause. This pattern, checking a condition and then acting on it as a separate step, is called check-then-act. Every lease or lock (a permission only one holder has at a time) has one. Seen from inside, a program is one continuous run of instructions. Seen from outside, it can stop between any two of them, for any length of time.

Checking again right before the write makes the gap smaller, but the pause can land right after the second check too. The fourth section measures how much that extra check buys. First, what stops a program, starting with the best-known cause.

sections.h: The garbage collector stops every thread, for far less time than it used to
sections.html:
The best-known reason a JVM thread stops is the garbage collector. A Kotlin or Java program creates objects all the time (a payment, a piece of text, a list) and never frees them itself. The JVM keeps them in an area of memory called the heap. The garbage collector is the part of the JVM that finds objects the program can no longer reach and frees their memory. To do that safely it must know which objects are still in use, and the program keeps changing that while it runs.

The simplest safe way is to stop every thread of the program while the collector looks. That's a stop-the-world pause. While it lasts, nothing of yours runs: not the code that writes updates, not the thread that renews the lease, not the heartbeat, the regular "I'm alive" message that tells other programs this one is still running (Detecting failure).

How long that takes depends on the collector and on how much of the heap is in use. The Try it measures three collectors that come with JDK 25, the current long-term version of Java. Each gets a 1 GB heap holding about 300 MB of objects that keep being replaced. On a laptop with 12 cores (a core is the part of a processor that runs one thread at a time):

  • Serial, which does all its work inside pauses, on one thread, stopped the world for 360 to 570 ms each time it tidied the whole heap.
  • G1, the default collector since JDK 9, does most of its searching while your threads run and pauses to move objects. Its longest pauses were 67 to 93 ms. (Its default target is 200 ms.)
  • ZGC's own log reported a longest pause of about 0.02 ms.

ZGC gets there by doing the expensive work, finding and moving objects, while your threads keep running. Its stated goal is never to stop the program's threads for more than a millisecond, however big the heap, from a few hundred megabytes to 16 TB. On JDK 25 the realistic choices are G1, or ZGC (or Shenandoah, a similar collector) when short pauses matter more than raw speed.

So ZGC makes the problem go away? Look at the Try it's other columns. ZGC's pauses were 0.02 ms, yet a thread that measured its own delays still saw stalls of 5 to 65 ms across runs. The collector isn't the only thing between a thread and a core. ZGC's own background threads, the program's other threads and every other program on the laptop compete for the same cores, and the operating system decides who runs next. And a program that creates objects faster than ZGC can free memory has to wait for it; ZGC logs these waits as allocation stalls.

A low-pause collector makes long pauses rarer. It doesn't make them impossible, and the causes in the next section don't care which collector you run.

try.title: Measure what each collector costs your thread
steps: Run the demo from the labs folder. It starts three separate JVMs with a 1 GB heap each, one per collector (Serial, G1 and ZGC). Each keeps about 300 MB of objects alive and replaces them at random for 2.5 seconds. Meanwhile one thread sleeps for 1 ms in a loop and records how late it wakes up: a stall it can feel. It takes about 10 seconds.
Before it finishes, predict the ZGC row: will the thread's longest stall match ZGC's longest pause from its own log?
Run it twice more and compare. Which numbers move, and which stay put?
try.expect:
One run on a 12-core MacBook with JDK 25:

collector   GC log: longest pause   your thread: longest stall   99.9th pct   stalls over 10 ms
Serial               360.763 ms                    360.7 ms      360.7 ms               7
G1                    89.390 ms                    103.4 ms       86.5 ms              24
ZGC                    0.022 ms                      8.7 ms        6.9 ms               0

Serial's pause is one long tidy-up of the whole heap, and the thread feels all of it. G1's pauses are shorter and more frequent. ZGC's log says its pauses were about 20 microseconds (millionths of a second), yet the thread still woke up 8.7 ms late at worst. The "99.9th pct" column is the 99.9th percentile: 999 of every 1,000 wake-ups were no later than that. In three runs here, Serial ranged from 360 to 570 ms and ZGC's thread stall from 9 to 62 ms, while ZGC's own pauses stayed near 0.02 ms. The GC log column, from the collector's own log, tells you about the collector; only a measurement from inside your thread tells you how long your code didn't run. Your numbers depend on the processor, the number of cores and what else the machine is doing.

refs.title: JEP 490: ZGC, remove the non-generational mode
JEP 363: remove the Concurrent Mark Sweep collector

aside.title: Can't we switch the garbage collector off?
aside.html: Almost. The JDK has a collector called Epsilon that hands out memory and never frees any. A program on it never pauses for a collection, and it crashes as soon as the heap is full. That suits a test or a program that runs for a few seconds, not a worker that runs for months. And the collector was never the only thing that can stop a program, as the next section shows.

sections.h: The cloud, the operating system and the disk can stop a program too
sections.html:
Every cause below stops a program from the outside, as the collector does, and none of them shows up as a garbage collection.

  • A shared machine. In the cloud, your server is usually a virtual machine: a pretend computer that runs, with others, on one real machine. A program called the hypervisor shares the real processor among them. While it runs another virtual machine on your core, yours stops. Linux, the operating system most servers run, counts that time as steal: the st column in top and vmstat, two commands that show what a machine is busy with. Clouds also move running virtual machines from one real machine to another. Google Compute Engine, Google's service that rents them out, says such a move typically pauses the machine for well under a second. It can also push the clock forward by up to 5 seconds.
  • A CPU quota. A container is a program walled off from others on the same machine, with limits on what it may use (Containers are processes: namespaces and cgroups). One limit is a share of processor time in each period, which is 100 ms long by default. A container that has used its share doesn't run again until the next period starts (CPU scheduling: EEVDF, nice and CPU quotas). If the JVM's collector threads use up the share early, every thread waits for the rest of the period.
  • Memory. When memory runs short, the operating system can move some of it out to disk, which is called swapping. Touching a piece that was moved means waiting for a disk read (Virtual memory: page tables, the TLB and page faults). A machine short of memory can spend most of its time waiting like this, so database and JVM servers usually run with swapping turned off.
  • Signals. A signal is a short message the operating system delivers to a program. SIGSTOP freezes it until SIGCONT arrives (Processes: fork, exec, wait and signals). Ctrl-Z in a terminal sends a close cousin with the same effect, so pressing it in the wrong window stops a program too. So does a debugger, a tool that lets a programmer halt a program and look inside.
  • The disk. A thread that writes and waits for the disk to confirm waits as long as the disk takes. If the disk is really reached over a network, as many cloud disks are, it waits for the network too.

The last one can hide inside what looks like a collection. Engineers at LinkedIn saw G1 pauses of 4.17 seconds on an 8 GB heap whose collections normally took under a second. An older collector paused for 11.45 seconds while using almost no processor time. The collector wasn't the problem. During each pause the JVM writes a line to its GC log (GC for garbage collection), a file that records every collection. That write was stuck behind other disk traffic. The kernel, the core of the operating system, was writing changed file data from memory out to the same disk (The page cache, writeback and fsync). In one reproduction, 1.47 s of a 1.59 s pause was the stuck write and 0.12 s was collection. Moving the GC log to tmpfs, a file system kept in memory, or to a faster disk brought every pause under 0.25 s.

The log line itself gives this away. With the JVM setting -Xlog:gc+cpu, every collection reports three times: User and Sys, the processor time spent in the program and in the kernel, and Real, the time on the clock. A collector that uses several threads normally uses more processor time than clock time. A pause whose Real is far above User plus Sys was spent waiting, not collecting.

One more detail matters for the Try it. A running program is called a process, and inside a container the first one to start gets process number 1. Linux protects process 1 from signals sent from inside the same container, unless it has asked to handle them. No program can ask to handle SIGSTOP, so kill -STOP 1 inside a container does nothing. From outside, docker pause freezes every program in the container at once (Docker is a tool that runs containers), and the programs can't tell.

So a program can be stopped by many things it never sees. Can it at least catch a pause itself, in time to hold back its write? That's next.

try.title: Freeze a lease holder from outside
steps: This one needs Docker and the lab box, the course's Linux container with the tools installed. From the labs folder, start PauseMeter in the lab box with the first command, in a container named pausebox. It holds a pretend 2-second lease and renews it below 1 second. Every 100 ms it checks the lease, works for 80 ms and "writes". The lease is a deadline on the monotonic clock, so it runs out on time even while the program is frozen, like a lease kept by another machine. It prints only when something unusual happens.

When it says Pause me now, freeze it from a second terminal, outside the container, with the two docker pause lines: once for 5 seconds, then for 3. Predict what it prints after each pause, and in which order.
Then run the last command. It tries to stop process 1 from inside a container, and then stops a JVM that isn't process 1.

code.title: terminal 1, from the labs folder
code.html: docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm --name pausebox box java sim/src/demo/java/sfz/dist/l04/demo/PauseMeter.java # terminal 2, on the Mac docker pause pausebox; sleep 5; docker unpause pausebox docker pause pausebox; sleep 3; docker unpause pausebox # afterwards, in one terminal docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box bash -c 'kill -STOP 1; echo "still running: PID 1 ignored SIGSTOP"; java sim/src/demo/java/sfz/dist/l04/demo/PauseMeter.java & sleep 3; kill -STOP $!; sleep 4; kill -CONT $!; sleep 2; kill $!'

From the two docker pause runs:

holding a 2 s lease; checking, working 80 ms and writing every 100 ms. Pause me now.
STALE WRITE: checked with 1,181 ms left, wrote 3,929 ms after the lease ran out.
loop gap: 5,147 ms since the last turn (expected 100). The wall clock moved 5,147 ms.
STALE WRITE: checked with 1,168 ms left, wrote 1,953 ms after the lease ran out.
loop gap: 3,143 ms since the last turn (expected 100). The wall clock moved 3,144 ms.

Both pauses happened to land during the 80 ms of work, between the check and the write, which is 80% of each turn. If yours lands in the other 20%, you see lease lost: it ran out ... ms ago instead, at the next check. Either way the program learns about the pause only after it runs again, and the stale write is reported before the gap, because the work that was under way finishes first. The wall clock, the time-of-day clock, moved as much as the monotonic one: a frozen container's clock keeps running. The last command prints still running: PID 1 ignored SIGSTOP, then a loop gap of about 4,000 ms and either a STALE WRITE or a lease lost line: kill -STOP works on the JVM, which is not process 1. (PID means process id, the number the operating system gives each running program.)

sections.h: Why a program can't catch its own pause in time
sections.html:
Can A protect itself? It has a monotonic clock and can read it after every step, and it does notice the pause: the next reading is 3 seconds later than the one before. But it notices afterwards, on the first instruction after the pause, and the step it was in the middle of runs first. Whatever was already decided, an update half built or a message already handed to the network, goes ahead. A program can measure its own pause exactly and still learn about it too late. Its sense of time passing is something it rebuilds each time it looks at the clock.

What A can do is make the gap smaller. The lab's careful worker does three things.

It counts its lease from the moment it sent the request, never from the moment it read the reply. The service starts the lease when the request arrives, which is after A sent it, so counting from the send can only make A's deadline earlier than the real one. The naive worker, the one from the first section, counts from the reply. Picture a renewal reply that arrives while A is frozen for 3 seconds and waits there to be read. The naive worker then believes it has 2 full seconds left on a lease that ran out while it was stopped. In the lab's run of that case, that one mistake causes 13 stale writes, writes that land after their lease ran out, in a row.

It checks again right before sending, after the work, as the second run of the first Try it showed. A pause during the 60 ms of work is caught there. Only a pause in the 5 ms after the last check gets through.

It keeps a margin: no write when less than the margin is left.

How much does that buy? The Try it runs the lab's sweep: pauses of one length, arriving at random about every 5 seconds on both workers, in 20 runs of ten minutes each. With 3-second pauses, the naive worker made 1,282 stale writes and the careful one 88, about 14 times fewer. The margin hardly mattered: 88 at 0, 200 and 500 ms. A worker that renews below 1 second always has 1 to 2 seconds left, so any pause that hurts is longer than that, and longer than any margin it could afford. A 10-second lease made 3- and 5-second pauses harmless and let 8-second ones through.

Every fix inside the worker moves the line. None removes it. A pause that starts after the last check and outlasts what is left of the lease always gets its write through. In the sweep, 64 of the careful worker's 88 stale writes landed on top of a newer holder's update. These fixes also pass every ordinary test, because tests don't freeze for 3 seconds at the worst moment. The lab has a test that freezes the worker at exactly that moment, and no change to the worker stops the late write.

If the worker can't stop itself in time, perhaps the pauses can be removed instead. Some systems do exactly that. Let's see what it costs.

sections.h: Systems that can't afford a pause, and why servers don't copy them
sections.html:
Some software can't accept any of this. A pacemaker that stops for a garbage collection, or a car's braking controller that waits behind a disk write, has failed at the one thing it is for. These are hard real-time systems: every response has a deadline, and a missed deadline counts as a failure of the whole system.

They meet their deadlines by removing the causes of pauses rather than living with them. A real-time operating system gives each task a guaranteed slice of processor time in every interval. Each routine has a known worst-case running time, and the system is designed so that the worst cases add up to less than the deadline. Memory is set aside up front, or freed by a collector whose work in each interval has a known limit. The hardware is dedicated, with nothing else running on it. Then long testing shows that the deadlines hold.

That costs a lot, and it lowers the amount of work done per second, because the system keeps spare capacity so that the worst case still fits. Real-time in this sense means predictable, not fast. It has nothing to do with the "real-time" updates of a web app. For a payments program running on rented cloud machines, it isn't an option. Servers have to assume that any program can stop at any instruction, for any length of time.

So the safety of a lease can't depend on the holder stopping in time. It has to be checked by something that doesn't freeze along with the holder, and the natural candidate is the thing being written. The ledger in this lesson accepted every write. In the next lesson, the lease service hands out a number that grows with every new lease. The ledger remembers the highest one it has seen, and refuses A's late write.

opening:
Picture a video call with a friend. Her picture freezes halfway through a sentence. Ten seconds later it moves again, and she finishes the sentence, answering a question everyone else has already moved past. From her side, nothing happened.

Programs freeze the same way, and they can't feel it either. Say a program asks "am I still allowed to change this record?", gets a yes, and then changes it. On a laptop, the question and the change run a millionth of a second apart, so it's easy to treat them as one step. Smart people do, because every test they run agrees with them.

In Clocks you can't trust, we learned to measure time with a clock that never jumps. Here the clocks are perfect, and the program still acts too late. In this lesson, we'll freeze a program on purpose, find out what freezes programs in real life, and measure how far a program's own checks can protect it. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a friend frozen on a video call. Worker A did the same: it checked its lease, froze for 3 seconds, and wrote 1.4 seconds after the lease ran out. Its own checks made that about 14 times rarer in the lab, and never impossible.

You can freeze a program yourself. In a Mac or Linux terminal, run ping 127.0.0.1, which sends your own computer a numbered message every second. Press Ctrl-Z, wait ten seconds, type fg, then stop it with Ctrl-C. The numbers carry on with no gap, and ping never noticed the missing seconds.

Next, we'll ask how the ledger can refuse a late write from a worker that doesn't know it's late.

compare.title: The naive worker and the careful one, from the lab

a.label: Naive
a.title: Policy.kt (given)
a.html: object Naive : HolderPolicy { // counts the lease from the moment it handled the reply override fun believedExpiry(sentAt: Long, handledAt: Long, ttlMs: Long) = handledAt + ttlMs // checks once, at the start of the tick override fun mayStartWork(now: Long, believedExpiry: Long) = now < believedExpiry // and never looks again before the write leaves override fun maySendWrite(now: Long, believedExpiry: Long) = true }

b.label: Careful
b.title: Policy.kt (your lab answer)
b.html: class Careful(val marginMs: Long) : HolderPolicy { // the service started the lease after sentAt, so this deadline is never late override fun believedExpiry(sentAt: Long, handledAt: Long, ttlMs: Long) = sentAt + ttlMs override fun mayStartWork(now: Long, believedExpiry: Long) = believedExpiry - now >= marginMs // look again after the work, as late as possible override fun maySendWrite(now: Long, believedExpiry: Long) = believedExpiry - now >= marginMs }

compare.note: Same loop, same pauses. The careful worker makes its deadline earlier on purpose, and moves its last check from before the 60 ms of work to after it, so a pause during the work is caught. In the lab's sweep that cuts stale writes about 14 times with 3-second pauses. Neither version can see a pause that starts after its last check, and that is where the remaining stale writes come from.

worked.title: A worker froze for 4 seconds: find out what froze it

steps.say: Start the JVM with a GC log that includes processor times, so each collection says how much of its pause was work. A collector that uses several threads normally uses more processor time than clock time: here 0.27 s of processor time (User plus Sys) in 0.03 s on the clock (Real). This line comes from the G1 run in the second Try it.
steps.code:
java -Xlog:gc,gc+cpu:file=/var/log/payments/gc.log ...

[0.268s][info][gc       ] GC(1) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 451M->306M(1024M) 36.061ms
[0.268s][info][gc,cpu   ] GC(1) User=0.21s Sys=0.06s Real=0.03s

steps.say: Now read a suspicious line the same way. A 4-second Real with almost no User or Sys means the threads were stopped and the collector was waiting. Ask what the JVM writes during the pause. If the GC log sits on a disk that other programs write to heavily, move it to tmpfs, a file system kept in memory, as LinkedIn did.
steps.code: -Xlog:gc,gc+cpu:file=/dev/shm/gc.log      # tmpfs: the log write can't block on disk writeback

steps.say: Check the container's CPU quota. Linux keeps it in the file cpu.max: here 50,000 µs of processor time in every 100,000 µs period, so half a processor. In a container limited that way and running a busy loop for 3 seconds, every one of 31 periods was throttled (stopped once its share ran out), 1.5 s in all: 50 ms of running, then 50 ms of nothing.
steps.code:
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max
50000 100000
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat
usage_usec 1561745
nr_periods 31
nr_throttled 31
throttled_usec 1510500
(output trimmed)

steps.say: Measure stalls from inside the program, the way the second Try it's measuring thread does, and report the worst one as a number someone watches. It catches every cause at once, including the ones no log mentions.
steps.code: val worstStallMs = AtomicLong() thread(isDaemon = true, name = "stall-meter") { while (true) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() Thread.sleep(1) val lateMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 - 1 worstStallMs.accumulateAndGet(lateMs, ::maxOf) // publish and reset it once a minute } }

steps.say: Write down the worst pause you've measured, then design as if the next one will be longer. Any check of a lease or a leader role stays an optimization, and the thing it protects must refuse writes from an old holder (the next lesson).
steps.code:
worst stall last 30 days: 4.2 s (GC log write behind writeback, fixed)
lease TTL: 10 s, renew below 5 s   -> pauses under 5 s are harmless
anything longer: the ledger must refuse the write

lab.title: Measure what pauses do to a lease holder
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. No Docker needed. All 15 fail with NotImplementedError, Kotlin's error for code that hasn't been written yet.

Read World.kt, which is given. It holds a lease service that grants 2-second leases with a new id each time, a ledger that accepts every write, and two workers (holders, in the code) that renew below 1 second and, every 100 ms, check, work for 60 ms and write. Every step of a worker goes through step(), so a step that falls due during a pause runs when the pause ends. Then read Naive in Policy.kt: it is the worker from the first section.

In Damage.kt, write staleWrites, the writes that landed when their lease was no longer valid. Judge each one by the lease service's record, at the moment it landed. Then write clobbers, the writes that landed after a write under a newer lease. The first three tests in DamageTest pass.

Write sweep, which runs the simulator for each pause length and adds up the stale writes. All of DamageTest passes: no stale writes with 250 ms pauses, more than 100 with 1.5-second pauses, and more again with 3-second ones.

In Policy.kt, write Careful's three functions. MitigationTest and PausePropertyTest pass. Read the test a pause after the last check gets through whatever the margin: no change to the worker can make it fail.
Experiment: make Careful.believedExpiry count from handledAt, the moment the reply was read, and see which test fails, and by how much.
hints: In clobbers, keep var newest = 0; a write with leaseId < newest is a clobber; then newest = maxOf(newest, w.leaseId).
pauseLengths.associateWith { p -> seeds.sumOf { s -> staleWrites(simulate(base.copy(seed = s, pauseMs = p), policy)).size } }.
Careful.believedExpiry is sentAt + ttlMs. Both checks are believedExpiry - now >= marginMs.

drill.title: The careful worker from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write the careful worker's three rules as a Kotlin class that implements HolderPolicy. Then add one comment saying which pause none of the rules can catch, and why.

answer.html: class Careful(val marginMs: Long) : HolderPolicy { // count from the send: the service started the lease later, so this is never late override fun believedExpiry(sentAt: Long, handledAt: Long, ttlMs: Long) = sentAt + ttlMs override fun mayStartWork(now: Long, believedExpiry: Long) = believedExpiry - now >= marginMs // check again after the work, right before sending override fun maySendWrite(now: Long, believedExpiry: Long) = believedExpiry - now >= marginMs } // A pause that starts after maySendWrite returns true and outlasts what is left of the lease: // no code of the holder runs during it, so nothing in the holder can stop the write it already decided to send.

recap: From outside, a program can stop between any two instructions for any length of time, and from inside it can't tell. Every check-then-act on a lease has a gap that a pause can land in.
The garbage collector's stop-the-world pause is the famous cause, and a shrinking one: on JDK 25, ZGC's own pauses are well under a millisecond and G1's are tens of milliseconds.

Other causes don't care about the collector: a shared cloud machine, a container's CPU quota, swapping, SIGSTOP, and waiting for the disk, such as LinkedIn's 4- to 11-second "GC" pauses that were log writes stuck behind disk traffic.
A program measures its own pause only after it runs again. Counting the lease from the send and checking again right before writing cut stale writes about 14 times in the lab.

The limit: a pause after the last check still gets through, whatever the worker does. Hard real-time systems remove pauses at a price servers don't pay, so the thing being written must refuse late writes (the next lesson).

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "We moved the payout worker to ZGC and renew its 10-second lease with 5 seconds to spare, so two workers can't write the same ledger any more." Explain what is still wrong, and what you would measure.
explain.answer: ZGC takes garbage collection off the list of long pauses, but not the other causes. The cloud moving the machine, the container running out of its CPU quota, swapping, a SIGSTOP or a write stuck behind a busy disk can each stop the worker for seconds, and none of them is a collection. Renewing with 5 seconds to spare makes any pause shorter than 5 seconds harmless, which is good, but a longer one still lets the lease run out while the worker is frozen. The worker can't notice in time: it checks the lease, freezes, and when it runs again it finishes the write it had already decided to make. Checking again right before writing makes the gap smaller, not zero. So I'd measure the longest stall from inside the program with a measuring thread, check throttling and steal time, and keep the GC log in memory on tmpfs. And I'd make the ledger refuse writes from an old lease holder, which is what fencing tokens do, so that a long pause costs a refused write instead of a wrong balance.

deeper.html:
Collector history, in brief. ZGC became ready for production use in JDK 15. JDK 21 made it generational, collecting young and old objects separately because most objects are thrown away soon after they're made; that has been the default since JDK 23, and JDK 24 removed the old mode. Shenandoah, OpenJDK's other low-pause collector, got a production generational mode in JDK 25. Concurrent Mark Sweep (CMS), the low-pause collector that old tuning guides still describe, was removed in JDK 14.

Time to safepoint. The JVM can only stop a thread at a safepoint, a spot in the code where it knows exactly which objects the thread is using. A stop-the-world pause starts once every thread has reached one, so a single slow thread holds up all the others. -Xlog:safepoint prints each safepoint with Reaching safepoint, At safepoint and Total in nanoseconds; in the Try it's G1 run, reaching took about 3 microseconds and the collection itself 36 ms. A thread stuck in a long loop with no safepoint check inside used to be the classic way to make reaching slow.

Pauses that stop only one thread. The first use of a class makes the JVM read it from a file on disk, and the first calls of a method run slowly in the interpreter until the JIT, the JVM's built-in compiler, turns them into machine code. Both happen at unpredictable moments early in a program's life, which is one reason a freshly started program answers its slowest requests more slowly than one that has been running a while.

Pauses that hide from you. docker pause uses a Linux feature called the cgroup freezer, and the frozen programs can't observe it. A laptop that sleeps with its lid closed is the same experiment at a larger scale: every program carries on afterwards, and only the clocks show that time passed.

The numbers to compare against. Jepsen, a project that tests databases by breaking them on purpose, tested the locks of etcd 3.4.3 in 2020 with 2-second leases, five clients and a pause every 5 seconds, and lost about 18% of the updates the lock was supposed to protect. The next lesson starts from that result. For the book's framing of pauses, leases and real-time systems, see Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 9.
